newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Italy looks to Europe for identity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Italy looks to Europe for identity.

text.p: When Italy celebrated 50 years as a republic in 1996, it marked the occasion with a night of the very best of Italian music at the presidential palace in Rome.
The gala ended not with the national anthem but with the strains of Ode to Joy, the unofficial anthem of the European Union, by that most German of composers, Ludwig van Beethoven.
Beethoven's Ode will sound out again next week when foreign ministers of the EU, the bloc's Commissioners and other European luminaries gather to mark another anniversary in Rome.

At Italy's suggestion, they will be celebrating the 40th anniversary on March 25 of the Treaty of Rome, the founding charter of the six-member European Economic Community signed in the Italian capital's Renaissance city hall.
Few peoples of the 15-nation Union which has grown from the original EEC feel as European as the Italians.
But an uneasy sense that their country may be left behind as another milestone approaches will lurk at the festivities like an unwelcome guest.
Economic and monetary union (EMU), Europe's planned single currency, is due to be launched in January 1999.
Some voices among EU member states, notably Germany, are publicly questioning Italy's economic fitness to help found the currency union, given the country's record of high public deficits and debt.
ITALIAN SENSE OF IDENTITY ROOTED IN EUROPE
The doubts have dealt a blow to self-esteem in Italy, a country whose sense of identity is rooted in Europe.
Politicians are alarmed by the prospect of exclusion not only because of the potential economic damage that would stem from the lira's absence from the first wave.

"The new Europe cannot be born without Italy...Europe is not just currency. Remember that a Europe deprived of the part most bound to its Latin culture is unthinkable," Prime Minister Romano Prodi said recently.
"Slowly but surely the sense of identity, the consciousness is growing that Germanic culture cannot, on its own, represent the whole of Europe," he said.
Prodi's language is not just rhetoric.

Academics say his and similar remarks reflect an identification with Europe rooted in history and reinforced by Italy's disastrous experiment with the militaristic nationalism of World War Two Fascist dictator Benito Mussolini.

"We never had intellectuals who defined themselves in national terms...a strong national culture never developed," said Stefano Bartolini, a professor of political sciences at the European University Institute in Florence.
"If you came to Italy after 1945, or even today, you would never find a politician starting or ending a speech with Viva Italia," he said.
"Italians, in a sense, would rather be governed from Brussels than from Rome."

The late unification of Italy, completed in 1870, strong local and regional traditions and a lack of faith in national institutions, deepened by political corruption, continue to weigh against a sense of state.

"Italians, in many ways, are not a nation, at least not in the sense that the British, the French, the Danish, the Dutch are...Therefore they find that the (European) community is less challenging to their own identity definition," said Bartolini.
"Being Italian means the countryside, the landscape, the style of life, the cuisine, the family, the soccer," he said.
"If you go to the United States and you ask an American what is America, it is the flag. There is no way that an Italian can identify with a piece of cloth."
COUNTRY SEES SELF AT FOREFRONT OF INTEGRATION
That outlook made Italy fertile ground for joining France and Germany in the push for European partnership 50 years ago.

Reeling from wartime defeat, their economy lagging behind the rest of Europe's, post-war Italy's founding fathers seized on the ideal as a means of modernising the country. It has since seen itself at the forefront of closer integration.
The meeting of foreign ministers that opened the way to the Treaty of Rome took place in Messina, Sicily, in 1955.

The Single European Act to create a single internal EU market was signed in Milan in 1985, the road to the Maastricht Treaty which set out the terms for EMU was opened at a summit in Rome in 1990 and, last year, EU countries began their negotiations on the latest reform of the EU's workings in Turin.

"In the years that have passed since our constitution came into force, Italy has undergone a profound modernisation, almost always in the sign of Europe," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said in a speech this week.
He proposed that a revised new constitution being discussed should cede areas of Italian sovereignty to the European Union.
He coupled his proposal with a warning that missing the EMU boat could unleash anti-European sentiment unseen until now in Italy.
"If we miss the objective, nationalistic reflexes against the presumed parties to blame for our exclusion could gain the upper hand," Dini said.
"It would become more difficult, if not impossible, to pursue a policy of catching up with the rest through further sacrifices."
Mutterings of animosity against Germany and the strict deficit target countries need to meet to join EMU are already being heard on the far left and hard right of Italy's parliamentary spectrum.
Political analysts say the grumbling is unlikely to turn into outright hostility to the EU. Dini's remarks were as significant, however, for his mention of sacrifice.

Prodi and his centre-left government have frequently played the European card to help push through unpopular budgetary measures and in their drive to reform Italy's creaking, inefficient machinery of governance and state.
This year they have imposed higher taxes to try to lower the budget deficit to EMU levels. While widely unpopular, the levies have not generated significant social unrest.

"The Italian state...frequently had to use Europe to call on people to do things which it knew they wouldn't do in the name of Italy...That still applies," said Patrick McCarthy, professor of European studies at the Johns Hopkins University in Bologna.
"The Italians all want to be in Europe. Why do they want to be in Europe? Because Europe is not like Italy," he said.
